question: Why do nurses give medications through an IV line instead of having the patient swallow a pill?

options.A: It lasts much longer in the bloodstream than oral pills.
options.B: It prevents all known systemic side effects from occurring.
options.C: It is completely painless for every patient receiving treatment.
options.D: It provides a much faster onset of drug action in the body.

explanation: Spot on! Because IV fluids go straight into the bloodstream, the body skips the digestive tract entirely and goes to work right away. You've got this! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with severe vomiting and dehydration. Why is an IV line started instead of just giving them oral rehydration drinks?

options.A: The patient's digestive tract cannot absorb any liquids safely.
options.B: Oral fluids take too long to reach the stomach lining.
options.C: IV fluids rapidly restore circulating blood volume and correct electrolytes.
options.D: Intravenous fluids taste much better than oral rehydration salts.

explanation: Great thinking! When someone is vomiting heavily, IV fluids are the quickest way to restore circulating blood volume and get their electrolytes balanced safely. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: Where is the median cubital vein located, which is a favourite spot for starting an IV?

options.A: Near the inside of the ankle joint
options.B: Along the lateral side of the upper arm
options.C: On the back of the hand
options.D: In the antecubital fossa of the elbow

explanation: Exactly! The median cubital vein sits right across the bend of the elbow (the antecubital fossa), making it super accessible for quick IV lines and blood tests. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: When you gently tap and feel a patient's arm to find a good vein, what should a healthy peripheral vein feel like?

options.A: A hard, rigid cord that does not bounce back
options.B: A soft, bouncy vessel that refills after being pressed
options.C: A deep vessel that cannot be felt but looks dark blue
options.D: A pulsing vessel that moves strongly under the finger

explanation: Spot on! Healthy veins feel spongy, elastic, and refill promptly with blood after you press them. You'll get great at spotting these on the ward! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which of these commonly used IV fluids is classified as an isotonic fluid?
explanation: Well done! Normal saline has a salt and water balance very close to human blood plasma, so it stays nicely inside the vessels without causing weird fluid shifts. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: A patient has severe brain swelling, and you need a fluid that will draw excess water out of the swollen cells and back into the bloodstream. What type of IV solution do you need?
explanation: You got it! Hypertonic fluids are concentrated, creating an osmotic pressure that pulls fluid out of tissue cells and safely back into the blood vessels. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why do we apply a tourniquet to a patient's arm before trying to insert an IV cannula?

options.A: To sterilize the outer skin surface before cleaning
options.B: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the limb
options.C: To numb the local skin area and reduce sharp pain
options.D: To trap venous blood and make the veins swell up

explanation: Exactly! The tourniquet pauses blood from returning to the heart, causing the veins underneath to plump up so they are much easier to see and feel. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why do nurses prefer to use a clear, transparent dressing over an IV insertion site?

options.A: It completely stops the patient from feeling any accidental movement pain.
options.B: It allows the nurse to inspect the skin for redness without removing the cover.
options.C: It keeps the cannula warm so the IV fluid flows much faster.
options.D: It permanently seals the vein shut so no blood can ever leak out.

explanation: Spot on! Clear dressings keep outside germs away while letting you quickly check the site for early signs of swelling or redness without peeling anything back. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: At what angle should you hold your needle when inserting a peripheral IV cannula through the skin?
explanation: Great job! A shallow 15 to 30-degree angle lets you glide smoothly into the vein without accidentally poking right through the back wall of the vessel. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: During an IV insertion, what lets you know for sure that your needle has successfully entered the vein?

options.A: The infusion bag begins to drip rapidly without any pressure.
options.B: The surrounding skin turns pale and cool to the touch.
options.C: The patient reports a sudden cooling sensation in the arm.
options.D: A flash of blood appears inside the flashback chamber of the device.

explanation: That's right! Seeing that little 'flash' of dark red blood in the chamber is the classic sign that you're in the vein. Beautiful work! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: When programming an electronic IV infusion pump on the ward, what unit of measurement do you normally use?
explanation: Spot on! Pumps are designed to deliver a precise volume of fluid every hour, so we program them in mL/hr. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: You need to run 1000 mL of normal saline over 8 hours using a manual gravity tubing set with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the approximate flow rate in drops per minute?
explanation: You're doing great with math! Multiply 1000 mL by 15 to get 15,000 drops, then divide by 480 total minutes (8 hours x 60 mins). That gives you roughly 31 drops per minute! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: As a student nurse, how often should you check and inspect an active peripheral IV site on your patient?

options.A: Once every 48 hours during dressing changes
options.B: Only when the patient complains of severe pain
options.C: Only when the infusion bag runs completely empty
options.D: At least once every nursing shift

explanation: Exactly! Regular checks each shift help you catch tiny problems like early swelling or soreness before they turn into bigger issues. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Why do nurses flush an intermittent IV line with normal saline right after giving a medication?

options.A: To clear remaining drug residue and prevent line clotting
options.B: To dilute any air bubbles that entered during the injection
options.C: To numb the vein so the patient feels less soreness
options.D: To cool down the internal walls of the plastic tubing

explanation: Well done! Flushing pushes any leftover medication completely through the catheter, keeping the line clear and preventing clots. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which of these signs is the classic giveaway that an IV has 'infiltrated' (leaked into the tissue)?

options.A: A warm, red, hard streak running all the way up the arm
options.B: Severe chest pain accompanied by audible lung crackles
options.C: Bright red bleeding gushing out around the plastic catheter
options.D: Swelling, coolness, and pallor around the insertion site

explanation: Spot on! When IV fluid leaks into the tissue instead of the vein, it makes the skin look pale, feel cool, and swell up. Time to restart the line! [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: A patient receiving a strong chemotherapy drug through a peripheral IV suddenly complains of a burning pain, and the area starts swelling up. What is your very first action?

options.A: Stop the infusion immediately and disconnect the tubing.
options.B: Flush the IV line rapidly with normal saline to clear the drug.
options.C: Massage the arm firmly to help the drug spread out faster.
options.D: Apply a cold ice pack directly over the swollen area.

explanation: Safety first! Stopping the infusion right away prevents any more harsh fluid from leaking into the tissue and causing damage. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: Why must you always inspect the tip of an IV catheter immediately after taking it out of a patient's arm?

options.A: To see if the patient's blood type has changed during therapy
options.B: To test the sterility of the plastic surface before disposal
options.C: To check if the plastic tip broke off inside the vein
options.D: To measure how much blood remains inside the hollow needle

explanation: Great nursing habit! Always check the removed cannula to make sure the entire plastic tip came out cleanly and nothing was left behind. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is the proper technique for pulling a peripheral IV cannula out of a patient's skin?

options.A: Pull it out smoothly and parallel to the skin surface.
options.B: Twist the catheter in a full circle before lifting it out.
options.C: Tug it quickly and firmly to make the removal as fast as possible.
options.D: Pull it straight up toward the ceiling at a sharp 90-degree angle.

explanation: You've got it! Pulling it out smoothly and low to the skin prevents unnecessary scratching or trauma to the fragile vein wall. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)
